solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Film about team's departure

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the film's letters go round the team's

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's film about the alien
a cricket or football team is an eleven, XI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A film about a sports team leaving, or a player quitting the side.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket or football side has eleven players, and the Roman numeral for eleven is the usual crossword team.
explanation.definitionFit: An exit is the act of leaving, the same as a departure.

clue.text: Nobody cross? Turn up the gas

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up makes it read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: none means not one person
an X is a cross

explanation.surface: If nobody is angry, turn up the gas fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry but is the letter X, and 'turn up the gas' is a domestic instruction hiding the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenon is a noble gas, element 54.

clue.text: Cloth's cut in this outbuilding

parts.note: surface reading: fabric being trimmed, perhaps in a workshop
setter's reading: the cloth is the clergy, and their cut is the tenth of produce owed to the church, stored in this barn

explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is a traditional name for the clergy, and their cut is the tithe, a tenth of farm produce once paid to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Tithe barns were large farm buildings where the church stored the tenth of produce it collected.

clue.text: Softest of shots, nothing to catch

indicators.note: something that catches another thing holds it inside, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: squat is slang for nothing at all, as in 'diddly squat'
a shy is a throw or shot, as at a coconut shy

explanation.surface: Picking out the gentlest of strokes, perhaps in tennis, with nothing worth catching.
explanation.walkthrough: SQUAT (US slang for nothing, as in diddly squat) catches SHIES. 'Shots' tempts thoughts of drop shots or of squash the game, but it means throws.
explanation.definitionFit: Squashy describes something soft and easily pressed, so the superlative matches softest.

clue.text: Midget couple described by agents as darlings

indicators.note: to describe can mean to trace round, so these words are drawn around by the outer one

parts.note: spies are secret agents
wee means tiny
to tie is to join or couple

explanation.surface: Spies give a pair of small people a sweet nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Midget' and 'couple' read as nouns but are an adjective (wee) and a verb (tie).
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetie pie is an affectionate term of address, so sweetie pies are darlings.

clue.text: Person won't start, having got to reflect, to do so?

definitions.text: Person won't start, having got to reflect, to do so?

indicators.note: a word that will not start loses its opening letter

parts.note: a human is a person

indicators.note: a reflection shows things the wrong way round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: had is the past form of have, meaning got

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot get going, stopping to think, would hesitate over it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a person who won't start speaking, pausing to reflect, makes those hesitating noises.
explanation.definitionFit: To um and ah is to hesitate or dither, making filler noises while thinking.

clue.text: One stupid assistant's run over

indicators.note: something run over is turned the other way, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: PA is a personal assistant, plus the S

explanation.surface: A dim helper has been knocked down by a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run over' looks like a road accident but signals the word read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A sap is a foolish, gullible person, so one who is stupid.

clue.text: Religion is mostly unconvincing

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a lame excuse is an unconvincing one

explanation.surface: A sceptic's verdict that a certain faith mostly fails to convince.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is the monotheistic faith founded on the teachings of Muhammad.

clue.text: Meets when its safe is blown

indicators.note: a safe that is blown is blasted apart, scattering its contents into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone gathers whenever a safe is blasted open in a robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'is' looks like grammar joining safe to blown, but it is part of the letter mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To satisfy a requirement is to meet it, as in meets the criteria.

clue.text: Curse stories associated with The Graduate

parts.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings about a person
taken as written
a Master of Arts is a graduate

explanation.surface: Tales linked with the film The Graduate are a curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Graduate' looks like the Dustin Hoffman film title, but it splits into an article and a degree holder.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is a formal ecclesiastical curse, or a thing cursed and loathed.

clue.text: One might support keeping it civil

indicators.note: keeping means holding on to, so one word holds the other within it

parts.note: a pole is something that holds things up
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who backs an argument might keep it courteous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One might support' is a cryptic description of a supporting pole, not a supporter in an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Polite and civil are synonyms, both meaning courteous in manner.

clue.text: "Skid" marks

parts.note: surface reading: tyre marks left on a road after skidding
setter's reading: the punctuation marks around the word skid, the quotes themselves

explanation.walkthrough: Skid marks suggest a road accident; the quotation marks round 'Skid' are the marks the clue is describing.
explanation.definitionFit: Inverted commas is the British name for quotation marks, which surround the word in the clue.

clue.text: Second pair of grouse shot — not so safe, then!

definitions.text: Second pair of grouse shot — not so safe, then!

indicators.note: the second pair of letters means the third and fourth, after the first two

parts.note: the third and fourth letters of the bird's name

indicators.note: shot means ruined or broken, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grouse shot at the wrong time of year is a risky business for the gun.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the meaning: grouse may only be shot in season (from 12 August), so shooting outside it is illegal and not safe for the shooter.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of season means outside the legal period for hunting a particular game bird or animal.

clue.text: Egyptian god embraced by smart priest

indicators.note: something embraced is held in another's arms, so it sits inside the other word

parts.note: cute can mean clever or shrewd
Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: An Egyptian deity being hugged by a smartly dressed priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' suggests well dressed, but here it means clever, as cute does in 'a cute move'.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate is a clergyman assisting a parish priest, so a priest of junior rank.

clue.text: Word perfect? Great to include noun

parts.note: utter means complete or absolute, as in perfect nonsense

indicators.note: including something means taking it in, so one word holds the other

parts.note: ace means excellent
N is the abbreviation for noun

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a speech is word-perfect, and is told it is great to add a noun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Word perfect' looks like one phrase but splits into the definition and UTTER.
explanation.definitionFit: An utterance is something spoken, a word or remark.

clue.text: Friend, welcome! Starts to exchange hostile correspondence

indicators.note: swapping the opening sounds of a pair of words is exactly what a spoonerism does

parts.note: a mate is a friend, and hail is a call of welcome; swap their first letters

explanation.surface: A friendly greeting that turns into nasty letters, a mixed message.
explanation.definitionFit: Hate mail is letters or messages sent to express hostility or abuse.

clue.text: Fine — wrong clue

parts.note: the dash is read as a minus sign

indicators.note: wrong means incorrect, so the letters are out of their right order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a crossword clue is incorrect, with the reply 'fine'.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash looks like punctuation, but it is a minus sign. Fine here means very thin or tiny, not okay.
explanation.definitionFit: Minuscule means extremely small, as fine does for very thin or delicate particles.

clue.text: Still in position

definitions.meaning: second meaning: upright and in place

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase, 'still in position', but splits into two meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing water is motionless, and a standing structure remains erect and in place.

clue.text: Force wife to share cost

parts.note: go can mean energy or drive
'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife, from duchess of Fife

explanation.surface: Making your wife pay her share of the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' for wife is Cockney rhyming slang: 'Duchess of Fife', shortened to 'my old Dutch'.
explanation.definitionFit: To go Dutch is to split a bill, each person paying their own share.

clue.text: Perfect angle in parts

indicators.note: parts as a verb means separates or opens up, making room for something to go between

parts.note: to angle is to fish with rod and line
taken as written

explanation.surface: A geometric angle being perfect in some sections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angle' tempts toward geometry but is the verb meaning to use a rod and line; 'parts' is also a verb, opening that word to let the next one in.
explanation.definitionFit: To perfect something is to give it its final polish, as in putting a finish on it.

clue.text: Some Christians prefer it over sin?

parts.note: these letters rearrange into a word naming a variant

explanation.surface: Some Christians favour a faith that is more against sin.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is itself an instruction read backwards: VERSION, revised, gives 'over sin'. The Revised Version is a Victorian English Bible translation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Revised Version is an English Bible translation still favoured by some churchgoers over others.

clue.text: Trumpet relative with higher volume

parts.note: V is the abbreviation for volume
an aunt is a family relative
positional only: in a down clue, the volume letter sits above the next piece

explanation.surface: A trumpet's cousin in the brass family, played louder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Higher' tells you, in a down clue, that V sits above AUNT. 'Trumpet' looks like the instrument but is the verb to boast.
explanation.definitionFit: To trumpet one's success is to boast loudly about it, which is what vaunt means.

clue.text: Our skirts certainly smell

indicators.note: to skirt something is to go round its edges, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: taken as written
do is an emphatic intensifier, as in 'I do like it'

explanation.surface: Our skirts definitely stink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirts' looks like clothing but is the verb, meaning goes round. DO stands for certainly as an emphatic, as in 'I do agree'.
explanation.definitionFit: An odour is a smell, usually a noticeable or unpleasant one.

clue.text: No more opera — I hate it

parts.note: ENO is English National Opera
ugh is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea from someone who cannot bear another night of opera.
explanation.walkthrough: ENO is English National Opera, the London company based at the Coliseum.
explanation.definitionFit: Enough as an exclamation means stop, I want no more of this.

clue.text: In the Midlands she drove most of the way

indicators.note: most of the way means stopping short of the end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: to herd cattle is to drive them

explanation.surface: A woman from the Midlands did most of the driving on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove' looks like driving a car but is herding animals. The Midlands is the central region of England.
explanation.definitionFit: In Midlands dialect 'her' is used as a subject pronoun, as in 'her's gone out' for she has.

clue.text: The heartless boss wants huge shelters

indicators.note: without its heart a word loses its middle, leaving just the outside letters

parts.note: the word with its centre removed
a boss is a raised knob or stud
OS stands for outsize

explanation.surface: A callous employer demands enormous sheds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like an employer but is the ornamental knob, a stud. A testudo was the Roman tortoise formation of overlapping shields.
explanation.definitionFit: A testudo was a protective cover, either a shield formation or a siege screen, so a shelter for troops.

clue.text: Above the tent, bar has come loose

indicators.note: something that has come loose is no longer fixed in place, so its letters are free to move

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Over a campsite tent, a pole has worked free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Above' looks like a position for the bar, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Better than and above both mean superior to, as in a cut above the rest.

clue.text: Win each service

parts.note: EA is the standard abbreviation for each
the Royal Navy is the senior armed service

explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests tennis after 'Win', but it is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn is to gain or obtain by merit, a sense of win.
